lesson_title: Pair Number Seven Thousand: Walking Paper 2
hook_text: A shoe factory makes 8 200 pairs — but only the last 1 200 of them earn a single cent.
clip_script: A shoe factory sells at two hundred and forty rand a pair. Each pair swallows one hundred and fifty in leather, labour and delivery before it earns anything — leaving ninety rand of contribution. But the factory itself demands six hundred and thirty thousand a year in rent, machines and salaries, sold pair or not. So march the pairs out the door one by one, each dropping its ninety rand toward that mountain. Pair one: the mountain barely notices. Pair five thousand: halfway. Pair seven thousand: the mountain is exactly paid off. That pair — number seven thousand — is the break-even pair. It earns nothing. It just opens the gate. From pair seven thousand and one, the full ninety rand is pure profit: this year's eight thousand two hundred pairs put twelve hundred past the line — one hundred and eight thousand rand of profit, no long table needed. Last year? Seven thousand five hundred pairs against a break-even of seven thousand six hundred. One hundred pairs short. A loss — and most of the class would have called a factory making seven and a half thousand pairs successful. Now the twist the examiner saves for the end: leather rises fifteen rand a pair. Contribution thins to seventy-five, and the gate slides to eight thousand four hundred — beyond everything the factory currently makes. Same machines, same workers, suddenly a loss-maker. That one moving line — contribution against fixed costs — is the heart of the whole managerial paper.
visual_style: Shoes marching along a mountain path dropping golden ninety-rand coins into a crevasse; the seven thousandth pair lights a green gate; a leather price spike visibly drags the gate further up the mountain.
mood: Cinematic, rhythmic, with a cold twist.
pacing: Marching build through the cohort of pairs, triumphant beat at the gate, ominous slide when the gate moves.
